title: Anatomical Planes, Directions & Movement Terms | Corpus
description: Learn foundational anatomical language, including standard anatomical position, sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes, directional pairs, and movements.
h1: Anatomical Language: Standard Position, Planes, Directions and Movements
blurb: The universal coordinate system of medicine: standard anatomical position, sagittal, coronal, and transverse planes, directional pairs, and joint movements.
lead: Without a shared coordinate system, 'left,' 'up,' or 'behind' would change every time a person rolled over—so anatomy begins with a universal map of planes and directions. In this illustrated guide to anatomical planes and directions, we examine 24 documented structures—including standard anatomical position, patient right and left, median sagittal plane, parasagittal plane—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Without a shared coordinate system, 'left,' 'up,' or 'behind' would change every time a person rolled over—so anatomy begins with a universal map of planes and directions. Anatomical terminology begins with the subject in anatomical position: upright, facing forward and palms anterior. Relative terms refer to the subject, not the observer. Median sagittal, coronal and transverse reference planes divide the body left-right, front-back and superior-inferior; parasagittal and oblique sections serve other views. Movements are defined about joints and their axes, with limb-specific terms including pronation, dorsiflexion and inversion. The translucent planes on this digitally rendered body are conceptual, not physical membranes. Imaging orientations must be confirmed for each modality. Within the human body, the anatomical language · planes & movement (Terminologia anatomica) is situated in whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes.

Structurally, the standard anatomical position comprises upright, face forward, upper limbs at sides with palms anterior and thumbs lateral; feet directed forward. Directions use the subject’s body, not the viewer’s. Physiologically, the standard anatomical position provides a consistent reference for locations and movements. Structurally, the patient right and left comprises right and left always refer to the subject; on an anterior image, patient right usually appears on the viewer’s left. Physiologically, the patient right and left prevents reversal when describing a structure or reading a map. Structurally, the median sagittal plane comprises vertical plane through the midline dividing the body into equal right and left halves. The translucent sheet is a conceptual aid. Physiologically, the median sagittal plane governs defines exact midline relationships. Structurally, the parasagittal plane comprises any sagittal plane parallel to but displaced from the midline, yielding unequal left and right portions. Physiologically, the parasagittal plane governs locates off-center section views. Clinically, regarding the median sagittal plane, do not confuse sagittal with a front-versus-back coronal section. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the frontal (coronal) plane, coronal scans can show both kidneys and the spine on one slice. In clinical pathology involving the transverse (axial) plane, image display orientation must be checked rather than guessed. Medical evaluation of the standard anatomical position also notes that prone or supine patients retain anatomical left and right.

questions.question: What is the standard anatomical position?
questions.answer: The subject stands upright facing forward, with arms at the sides and palms facing anteriorly; thumbs point laterally. Right and left always belong to the subject, even when a patient is lying down. Structurally, the standard anatomical position comprises upright, face forward, upper limbs at sides with palms anterior and thumbs lateral; feet directed forward. Directions use the subject’s body, not the viewer’s. Physiologically, the standard anatomical position provides a consistent reference for locations and movements.

questions.question: How do sagittal, coronal and transverse planes differ?
questions.answer: A sagittal plane separates right from left, a coronal plane separates anterior from posterior, and a transverse plane separates superior from inferior. The median sagittal plane passes through the midline. Structurally, the median sagittal plane comprises vertical plane through the midline dividing the body into equal right and left halves. The translucent sheet is a conceptual aid. Physiologically, the median sagittal plane governs defines exact midline relationships.

questions.question: What is the difference between proximal and distal?
questions.answer: Proximal means closer to the point where a limb joins the trunk; distal means farther from that attachment. The elbow is proximal to the wrist in the upper limb. Structurally, the proximal and distal comprises proximal is nearer a limb’s attachment to the trunk; distal farther away along the limb. Physiologically, the proximal and distal governs describes relative position along a limb.

questions.question: Why does patient right appear on the left side of a front-facing illustration?
questions.answer: An anterior image faces the patient. Their right side is therefore on the observer’s left. Anatomical descriptions use the patient’s own side, not the screen’s left or right. Structurally, the patient right and left comprises right and left always refer to the subject; on an anterior image, patient right usually appears on the viewer’s left. Physiologically, the patient right and left prevents reversal when describing a structure or reading a map.

questions.question: Are the colored planes in this atlas real body membranes?
questions.answer: No. The translucent sheets are computer-generated reference planes used to explain sections. They are not physical tissues, and the chapter does not place false anatomical pins on them. Structurally, the frontal (coronal) plane comprises vertical plane dividing anterior and posterior portions; shown by a translucent sheet, not a real tissue boundary. Physiologically, the frontal (coronal) plane governs organizes front-to-back relationships.
